chapter.title: Set the pace

cards.body: Picture leading a friend along a cliff path. If you rush, they stumble and stop looking at the view. If you keep saying "um, so, like" at every turn, they can't tell which steps matter. **A good leader walks a little slower than feels natural and lets the silence do the pointing.**
cards.simpler: Imagine walking a friend along a cliff path. Go too fast and they trip, and they stop looking at the view. Say "um, so, like" at every step and they can't tell which steps matter. **A good guide walks a little slower than feels normal and lets the quiet do the pointing.** The same is true when you speak to a group. Slow down, and let the gaps show people where the important parts are.

cards.prompt: Priya is giving her 3-minute talk about why the office should adopt a 4-day week. Her mouth is dry, her heart is going, and she notices she's talking fast. What's most likely to help right now?

options.text: Speed up a bit more so she gets to the end before the nerves win
Slow down until it feels slightly too slow, and pause at the end of each sentence
Add a few "so" and "basically" to buy thinking time between points

whyNot.a: That's the nerves talking, not the listener: speeding up makes the walk harder for everyone following you.
whyNot.c: That's filler, not a pause: words like "so" and "basically" fill the gap but give the listener nothing to hold on to.

cards.reteach: Nerves push your speech faster. Your listeners need the opposite: a pace that feels a little slow to you is about right for them. The silence at a full stop is not a mistake. It's the moment they catch up.

cards.title: Slower than feels natural
cards.body:
When you're nervous, the speed that feels normal to you is faster than your listeners want. They are hearing your idea for the first time. You've heard it 20 times. **Aim for a pace that feels slightly too slow to you.** That's about right for them.

The easiest way to slow down is not to drag out words. It's to *pause at the full stops*: when a sentence ends, stop talking for a beat before starting the next one. One breath. Then go.

The pause feels long from the inside. From the outside it reads as calm.
cards.simpler:
When you are nervous, the speed that feels normal to you is too fast for the people listening. They are hearing your idea for the first time. You have heard it twenty times. **Aim for a pace that feels a bit too slow to you.** That is about right for them.

Don't drag out your words. Instead, stop for one breath at the end of each sentence. Then go on. The pause feels long to you. To them it sounds calm.

cards.title: Marcus and the one-minute recording
cards.body:
Marcus recorded himself talking for 1 minute about his cycling club's new route. He played it back and counted: 14 "ums", 6 "sos", 3 "likes". That's 23 fillers in 60 seconds, roughly one every 3 seconds.

On his second take he did one thing differently: every time he felt an "um" coming, he closed his mouth instead. He got it down to 9. It felt painfully slow while he was doing it. On playback, it sounded like someone who knew what he was talking about.
cards.simpler:
Marcus recorded himself for one minute talking about his cycling club's new route. He played it back and counted: 14 ums, 6 sos, 3 likes. That is 23 fillers in 60 seconds, about one every 3 seconds.

On his second try he changed one thing. **Each time he felt an um coming, he closed his mouth instead.** He got down to 9. It felt very slow while he did it. On playback, he sounded like someone who knew his subject.

cards.prompt: Dev is practising a line: "The route is 12 miles. Um, so, it starts at the station." Which version applies the chapter's idea?

options.text: "The route is 12 miles. [pause] It starts at the station."
"The route is 12 miles and so it starts at the station."
"The route is 12 miles, right, basically it starts at the station."

whyNot.b: That's joining two sentences, not pausing: the "and so" removes the full stop you were meant to rest on.
whyNot.c: That's swapping one filler for another: "right" and "basically" are the same gap-fillers wearing different clothes.

cards.reteach: Fillers show up where a pause should be. The fix isn't a better filler. It's silence. Say the sentence, close your mouth, breathe, then say the next one.

cards.title: Replace filler with silence
cards.body:
Fillers are the sounds you make while your brain finds the next word: "um", "so", "like", "basically", "you know". They're not a character flaw. They're a *gap-filling reflex*, and almost everyone has it.

**You don't remove fillers by trying harder. You replace them with a closed mouth.** When you feel one coming, shut your lips and let the gap be silent. The gap is the same length. It just has nothing in it.

The silence feels naked at first. Your listeners don't hear naked. They hear a person choosing their words.
cards.simpler:
Fillers are the little sounds you make while your brain looks for the next word: um, so, like, you know. Almost everyone has this habit of filling gaps.

**You don't get rid of fillers by trying harder. You swap them for a closed mouth.** When you feel one coming, shut your lips and let the gap stay quiet. The gap is the same length, just empty. It feels bare to you. Listeners hear a person choosing their words.

cards.body: Jo decided to fix her fillers by watching for them during her real talk. Every time she said "um", she winced and lost her thread. She finished with more fillers than she started with. The fix isn't vigilance on the day. It's practice on a recording beforehand, where you can hear yourself and try again. If you catch yourself policing your own speech mid-talk, that's the sign you skipped the recording step.
cards.simpler: Jo tried to fix her fillers by listening for them during her real talk. Each time she said um, she winced and lost her place. She ended with more fillers than she started with. **The fix is not watching yourself on the day. It is practice on a recording beforehand.** There you can hear yourself and try again. If you catch yourself policing your own speech mid-talk, you skipped the recording step.

cards.prompt: A friend says: "I want to sound more confident when I speak. What's the one thing you'd change?" Which answer matches this chapter?

options.text: Speak faster so you sound sure of yourself
Memorise your talk word for word so there are no gaps
Go slower than feels right, and let the gaps be silent instead of filling them

whyNot.a: That's the opposite of the chapter's advice: speed reads as nerves to a listener, not confidence.
whyNot.b: That's chapter 7's rehearsal idea, not pacing: memorising doesn't stop fillers, and it makes you more likely to speed through.

cards.reteach: Confidence sounds like someone who isn't in a hurry. Slow down to the point of discomfort, pause at full stops, and when a filler wants to come out, close your mouth instead.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **Talk slower than feels natural and pause at every full stop.** When an "um" or "so" wants to come out, close your mouth and let the silence sit there instead.
cards.simpler: Here is the whole chapter in one breath. **Talk slower than feels natural and pause at every full stop.** When an um or so wants to come out, close your mouth and let the silence sit there instead. The pause feels long to you. To your listeners it sounds like calm. That is all you need to remember.

cards.body: Open your phone's voice recorder. Talk for 1 minute about what you did today. Play it back and count the fillers. Record again, closing your mouth at each gap. Compare the two numbers.
cards.simpler: Open the voice recorder on your phone. Talk for one minute about what you did today. Play it back and count every um, so and like. Then record again. **This time, close your mouth at each gap instead of making a sound.** Count the fillers again and compare the two numbers. Two minutes of talking shows you exactly where you stand.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now record yourself for 1 minute, count your fillers, and halve them on a second take.
